questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A moss sporophyte remains attached to a green gametophyte. When transfer of organic nutrients from the gametophyte is blocked, the sporophyte stops growing despite light and water. Which inference is best supported?
options: A) Its sporophyte depends nutritionally on the gametophyte
B) Its sporophyte is the only photosynthetic generation
C) Its gametophyte is always diploid
D) Spores cannot form by meiosis
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Nutritional dependence on the gametophyte.
Why: The intervention leaves external light and water available but blocks the transfer route from the attached gametophyte. Arrested growth therefore supports dependence on its parent tissue for at least some resources. It does not prove complete absence of sporophyte photosynthesis; the comparison isolates nutrient support.
Why not the others: (B) overclaims exclusive photosynthesis; (C) confuses the haploid gametophyte with diploid sporophyte; (D) concerns a later spore-production mechanism not tested here.
Key point: Use the controlled change to identify dependence, not every metabolic capacity.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.topic: Structural Organisation In Plants And Animals
questions.sub_topic: Ovary position and plants that show it
questions.question: The flower section in the figure places sepals, petals and stamens above an ovary with two chambers. Which pair of plants has flowers with this position of the ovary?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Guava and cucumber.
Why: In the figure the sepals, petals and stamens arise above the ovary, so the ovary is inferior and the flower is epigynous. This happens when the margin of the thalamus grows upward, encloses the ovary completely and fuses with it. Guava and cucumber are the standard examples, along with the ray florets of sunflower.
Why not the others: (A) Mustard and china rose are hypogynous: the gynoecium is at the top and the other parts arise below it, so the ovary is superior. (C) Plum and peach are perigynous: the gynoecium is in the centre and the other parts arise on the rim of the thalamus at about the same level, so the ovary is half inferior. (D) Brinjal and mustard are both hypogynous.
Key point: Hypogynous: superior ovary (mustard, china rose, brinjal). Perigynous: half inferior (plum, rose, peach). Epigynous: inferior (guava, cucumber).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A membrane protein moves solute X inward even when inward X concentration exceeds the outside. A respiratory inhibitor stops the inward accumulation, but a separate dye confirms the membrane remains intact. Which mechanism is most consistent?
options: B) Facilitated diffusion down X's gradient
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Energy-coupled active transport.
Why: Accumulation against X's concentration gradient needs an energy source or coupling to another downhill gradient. The inhibitor removes the inward movement while membrane integrity persists, supporting an energy-dependent carrier rather than leakage or destruction of the barrier. The second dye control is needed to distinguish transport loss from membrane rupture.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) cannot drive X uphill by its own gradient; (D) concerns water rather than X accumulation.
Key point: Combine gradient direction with an energy and integrity control.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: In matched leaves, a C₃ leaf fixes 120 units of carbon but loses 30 units to photorespiration; a C₄ leaf fixes 100 units and loses 5. Ignoring other losses, which has higher net carbon gain and by how much?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) C₄ by 5.
Given: C₃ leaf: fixes 120 units, loses 30 to photorespiration. C₄ leaf: fixes 100 units, loses 5.
Formula/Principle: Net carbon gain = carbon fixed − carbon lost.
Step 1: C₃ net = 120 − 30 = 90 units.
Step 2: C₄ net = 100 − 5 = 95 units.
Step 3: Difference = 95 − 90 = 5 units in favour of the C₄ leaf.
Why: In C₃ plants, Rubisco also reacts with oxygen, and the resulting photorespiration gives back some of the carbon already fixed. C₄ plants concentrate CO₂ around Rubisco in the bundle-sheath cells, so photorespiration is very low. A leaf that fixes less carbon in total can therefore end with more.
Why not the others: (A) "C₃ by 20" compares only the gross amounts fixed (120 and 100). (B) "C₃ by 5" has the right difference but gives it to the wrong leaf. (C) "C₄ by 20" uses the gross difference and reverses it.
Key point: Compare net gains, not gross fixation.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: Which blood vessel carries oxygenated blood from the lungs to the heart?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Pulmonary vein.
Why: Blood is oxygenated in the lungs and returns to the left atrium of the heart through the pulmonary veins. Veins are vessels that carry blood towards the heart, whatever its oxygen content, so the pulmonary veins are veins that carry oxygenated blood.
Why not the others: (B) The pulmonary artery carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle to the lungs. (C) The superior vena cava brings deoxygenated blood from the upper body to the right atrium. (D) The coronary sinus drains deoxygenated blood from the heart wall into the right atrium.
Key point: Arteries carry blood away from the heart and veins towards it; the pulmonary vessels are the exception in oxygen content.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Number of meiotic divisions needed for seed formation
questions.question: In an angiosperm, each seed needs one pollen grain and one functional megaspore. One microspore mother cell gives four pollen grains, and one megaspore mother cell gives one functional megaspore. What is the minimum number of meiotic divisions needed to produce 100 seeds?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 125.
Given: 100 seeds need 100 pollen grains and 100 functional megaspores.
Formula/Principle: One meiosis in a microspore mother cell gives 4 pollen grains. One meiosis in a megaspore mother cell gives 4 megaspores, of which only 1 is functional.
Step 1: Meiotic divisions for pollen = 100 ÷ 4 = 25.
Step 2: Meiotic divisions for megaspores = 100 ÷ 1 = 100.
Step 3: Total = 25 + 100 = 125.
Why: The two sides of the count differ because all four products of male meiosis are used, whereas three of the four megaspores degenerate. Each ovule therefore needs its own meiosis, but four pollen grains share one.
Why not the others: (A) 100 counts only the female side. (C) 200 assumes one meiosis for each pollen grain as well as each egg. (D) 50 assumes four functional megaspores per meiosis as well as four pollen grains.
Key point: Meioses for n seeds = n + n/4.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A dihybrid AaBb is test-crossed to aabb. Genes assort independently. Among offspring that show the dominant A phenotype, what fraction also shows dominant B?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1/2.
Given: AaBb × aabb; the two genes assort independently.
Formula/Principle: A test cross gives four equally frequent classes. Conditional probability = P(both) ÷ P(condition).
Step 1: Offspring: AaBb, Aabb, aaBb, aabb, each 1/4.
Step 2: P(dominant A phenotype) = 1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2.
Step 3: P(dominant A and dominant B) = 1/4.
Step 4: P(dominant B | dominant A) = (1/4) ÷ (1/2) = 1/2.
Why: Because the genes assort independently, knowing the phenotype for gene A tells nothing about gene B. So the chance of the dominant B phenotype stays at one half, whichever A class is looked at.
Why not the others: (A) 1/4 is the chance of both dominant phenotypes among all offspring, without the condition. (B) 1/3 uses three classes in the denominator instead of the two A-dominant classes. (D) 3/4 is the dominant fraction from a monohybrid F₂, not from a test cross.
Key point: For independent genes, P(B | A) = P(B).

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A pathogen is cleared from immunised mice. Transferring purified serum to naive mice fails to protect, but transferring antigen-experienced T lymphocytes protects; heat-treated T cells are a negative control. Which defence is most directly implicated?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Cell-mediated adaptive immunity.
Why: Protective activity follows viable antigen-experienced T cells rather than the transferred antibody-containing serum. The heat-treated control makes nonspecific material carried with the cells less plausible. This supports a cellular effector or helper mechanism; it does not claim antibodies never contribute in other infections.
Why not the others: (A) predicts serum protection; (B) does not explain the T-cell-specific transfer result; (C) assigns immune specificity to erythrocytes.
Key point: Use transfer and viability controls to locate the protective arm.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A PCR forward primer binds the bottom template just left of a target region. Which orientation must a reverse primer have on the top strand to amplify the bounded segment over cycles?
options: A) Its 3′ end points toward the forward primer and target interior
B) Its 5′ end points toward the target interior
C) Both primers bind the same strand facing right
D) A reverse primer is unnecessary after the first cycle
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) The reverse primer's 3′ end faces inward.
Why: Polymerase extends only from primer 3′ ends, so the two primers must face each other across the segment on opposite templates. Outward-facing reverse extension would copy away from the bounded target and not yield exponential accumulation of that product.
Why not the others: (B) confuses 5′ orientation with extension direction; (C) loses opposite-strand bounding; (D) ignores recurring priming each cycle.
Key point: Draw both 3′ ends pointing into the amplicon.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A producer population captures 900 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ as gross primary productivity and uses 350 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹ in its own respiration. What is its net primary productivity?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 550.
Given: Gross primary productivity = 900 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹; respiration by the producers = 350 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Formula/Principle: Net primary productivity = gross primary productivity − respiration (NPP = GPP − R).
Step 1: NPP = 900 − 350 = 550 kJ m⁻² yr⁻¹.
Why: Gross primary productivity is the rate at which producers fix energy. Part of it is used at once in their own respiration. What is left is stored as new biomass and is the energy available to herbivores and decomposers.
Why not the others: (A) 350 is the respiration loss. (C) 900 is the gross value, before respiration is taken off. (D) 1250 adds the respiration instead of subtracting it.
Key point: NPP = GPP − R.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A woman is heterozygous for an X-linked recessive allele and her partner is affected. Given that their daughter is unaffected, what is the probability she is a carrier?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 1.
Given: Mother XᴬXᵃ (carrier); father XᵃY (affected); the daughter is unaffected.
Formula/Principle: Every daughter receives the father's only X chromosome.
Step 1: From the father every daughter gets Xᵃ.
Step 2: From the mother a daughter gets Xᴬ or Xᵃ, each with probability 1/2, giving XᴬXᵃ (unaffected) or XᵃXᵃ (affected).
Step 3: An unaffected daughter must be XᴬXᵃ, which is a carrier.
Why: The father's X carries the recessive allele and all his daughters inherit it. An unaffected daughter is unaffected only because her mother gave her the normal allele; she still has her father's allele. So the information "unaffected" leaves only one possible genotype.
Why not the others: (A) 0 ignores the allele that comes from the father. (B) 1/2 is the fraction of all daughters who are carriers, before using the fact that this daughter is unaffected. (D) 2/3 is the carrier chance for an unaffected child of two carriers in an autosomal cross, which does not apply here.
Key point: An affected father makes every daughter at least a carrier.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: A two-gene test cross yields parental classes 420 and 380, and recombinant classes 110 and 90. What is the recombination fraction and which conclusion is warranted?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 20%; linkage with recombination.
Given: Parental classes 420 and 380; recombinant classes 110 and 90.
Formula/Principle: Recombination frequency = recombinant offspring ÷ total offspring × 100.
Step 1: Total = 420 + 380 + 110 + 90 = 1000.
Step 2: Recombinants = 110 + 90 = 200.
Step 3: Recombination frequency = 200 ÷ 1000 = 0.20 = 20%.
Why: If the two genes assorted independently, all four classes would be about equal and the recombinants would be 50%. Here the parental classes are far more common, so the genes are on the same chromosome. Linkage is not complete, because recombinants do appear: crossing over between the genes produces them in 20% of the gametes.
Why not the others: (A) 10% counts only one of the two recombinant classes, and complete linkage would give no recombinants at all. (B) has the right value but 20% is well below the 50% expected for independent assortment. (C) 50% is not what the data show.
Key point: Recombination frequency below 50% means linkage; 0% means complete linkage.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Minute ventilation and air reaching the alveoli
questions.question: A resting person breathes 15 times per minute with a tidal volume of 500 mL. Of each breath, 150 mL stays in the conducting airways (nose to bronchioles), where no gas exchange occurs. How much fresh air reaches the alveoli each minute?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 5.25 L.
Given: Breathing rate 15 per minute; tidal volume 500 mL; 150 mL of each breath stays in the conducting airways.
Formula/Principle: Air reaching the alveoli per minute = (tidal volume − volume left in the airways) × breathing rate.
Step 1: Air reaching the alveoli per breath = 500 − 150 = 350 mL.
Step 2: Per minute = 350 × 15 = 5250 mL = 5.25 L.
Why: The trachea, bronchi and bronchioles only conduct air; exchange of gases happens in the alveoli. The last part of each breath never gets past the conducting airways and is breathed out again unchanged, so it must be left out of the count.
Why not the others: (B) 7.50 L is the total air breathed per minute (500 × 15), including the part that never reaches the alveoli. (C) 2.25 L is the part that stays in the airways (150 × 15). (D) 9.75 L adds the two volumes instead of subtracting.
Key point: Useful ventilation = (tidal volume − airway volume) × rate.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.sub_topic: Effect of enzyme concentration at saturating substrate
questions.question: With substrate at a saturating concentration, an enzyme preparation gives an initial rate of 50 units. The amount of enzyme is doubled, and the substrate is still saturating. A separate set of measurements finds the substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate, before and after doubling. What is expected?
options: A) The rate stays at 50 units; the half-maximal substrate concentration doubles
B) The rate rises to about 100 units; the half-maximal substrate concentration is unchanged
C) The rate rises to about 100 units; the half-maximal substrate concentration halves
D) The rate falls to 25 units; the half-maximal substrate concentration is unchanged
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) The rate rises to about 100 units; the half-maximal substrate concentration is unchanged.
Why: When substrate is saturating, every enzyme molecule is working at its full rate, so the maximum rate is proportional to the number of enzyme molecules. Doubling the enzyme doubles the maximum rate to about 100 units. The substrate concentration that gives half the maximum rate (the Michaelis constant, Kₘ) describes how readily one enzyme molecule binds its substrate. It is a property of the enzyme and does not depend on how many molecules are present.
Why not the others: (A) keeps the rate fixed, which would be true only if substrate, not enzyme, were limiting. (C) has the right rate but wrongly changes the half-maximal concentration; more enzyme does not change the affinity of each molecule. (D) a fall in rate has no basis when more catalyst is added.
Key point: Vmax ∝ enzyme concentration; Kₘ is independent of it.

questions.subject: Biology
questions.question: The gel figure shows a 5 kb DNA molecule uncut in lane U. After restriction enzyme E, the normal molecule gives 3 kb and 2 kb bands; a mutant sample gives only a 5 kb band. Assuming complete digestion in both samples, what changed?
options: A) An extra E recognition site appeared
B) The mutant molecule shrank to 2 kb
C) The E site was lost or altered in the mutant
D) The enzyme was absent from the mutant reaction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The E recognition site was lost or altered.
Why: Normal digestion divides the 5 kb molecule into fragments whose lengths sum to 5 kb. A mutant that remains 5 kb under the same complete-digestion control no longer presents the cuttable site. The control rules out simply blaming an inactive enzyme in that lane.
Why not the others: (A) would add smaller fragments; (B) contradicts the 5 kb band; (D) contradicts the stipulated complete digestion control.
Key point: Compare fragment sum and the controlled enzyme condition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Axial and equatorial bonds in PCl₅
questions.question: In gaseous PCl₅ the phosphorus atom has five bond pairs and no lone pair. What is the shape of the molecule, and how do its P–Cl bonds compare?
options: A) Square pyramidal; all five bonds are equal
B) Trigonal bipyramidal; all five bonds are equal
C) Trigonal bipyramidal; the three equatorial bonds are longer than the two axial bonds
D) Trigonal bipyramidal; the two axial bonds are longer than the three equatorial bonds
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Trigonal bipyramidal; the two axial bonds are longer than the three equatorial bonds.
Why: Five bond pairs around phosphorus are arranged as far apart as possible, which gives a trigonal bipyramid (sp³d hybridisation). The five positions are not equivalent. Each axial bond pair has three equatorial pairs at 90°, while each equatorial pair has only two neighbours at 90° and two at 120°. The axial pairs are repelled more strongly, so the axial bonds are slightly longer and weaker.
Why not the others: (A) A square pyramid is the shape for five bond pairs plus one lone pair, as in BrF₅. (B) has the right shape, but the axial and equatorial bonds are not equal. (C) reverses the comparison; it is the axial bonds that are longer.
Key point: In a trigonal bipyramid, axial bonds are longer than equatorial bonds.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Geometrical and optical multiplicity of a chelated octahedron
questions.question: The diagrams show the two geometrical arrangements of octahedral \([\ce{Co(en)2Cl2}]^+\), with each en joining two adjacent donor sites. Counting mirror-image forms separately but ignoring conformers, how many configurational stereoisomers exist in total, and how many of them are optically active?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Three total, of which two are optically active.
Given: The two chloride sites can be adjacent or opposite; en is bidentate and its donor pairs remain connected as shown.
Formula/Principle: Count geometrical arrangements first, then distinguish non-superposable mirror partners within each.
Step 1: Adjacent chlorides define the cis arrangement; opposite chlorides define trans.
Step 2: The cis arrangement has two non-superposable mirror forms because of the connected chelate rings.
Step 3: The trans arrangement has a symmetry plane and contributes one achiral form.
Step 4: Total \(=2+1=3\); optically active forms \(=2\).
Why: A ligand count or high/low-spin comparison cannot decide this stereochemical count. The chelate connections in the diagram must be preserved when testing whether a mirror image can be rotated onto the original.
Why not the others: (B) counts geometries but merges the cis mirror pair; (C) incorrectly splits trans into an optical pair; (D) treats the trans form as chiral.
Key point: Count geometry and optical multiplicity in separate stages.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Which order of carbon–oxygen bond length is correct for CO, CO₂ and CO₃²⁻?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) CO < CO₂ < CO₃²⁻.
Why: Bond length decreases as bond order increases. Carbon monoxide has a triple bond (bond order 3). In carbon dioxide each C–O bond is a double bond (bond order 2). In the carbonate ion the three C–O bonds are equivalent by resonance, each with bond order 4/3. So the bond is shortest in CO, longer in CO₂ and longest in carbonate.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the order, as if a higher bond order gave a longer bond. (C) places CO₂ shorter than CO, although a double bond is longer than a triple bond. (D) ignores the different bond orders.
Key point: Higher bond order → shorter, stronger bond.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An atom has three electrons in a set of three degenerate p orbitals. Which lowest-energy occupancy follows Hund's rule before pairing?
options: A) One orbital doubly occupied, one singly, one empty
C) One electron in each orbital with parallel spins
D) Three electrons in one orbital
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) One parallel-spin electron in each p orbital.
Why: Filling degenerate orbitals singly with parallel spins maximises exchange stabilisation before pairing costs energy. The three p orbitals are distinct spatial states; Pauli's rule also forbids three electrons in a single orbital. The energy comparison assumes no external splitting that destroys degeneracy.
Why not the others: (A) pairs prematurely; (B) requires six electrons for three pairs; (D) violates the two-electron orbital limit.
Key point: Apply Hund before pairing in equal-energy orbitals.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.topic: Organic Chemistry – Some Basic Principles and Techniques
questions.question: Which carbocation can delocalise its positive charge into an adjacent benzene π system, unlike an ordinary primary alkyl carbocation?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Benzyl cation.
Why: The positively charged benzylic carbon has an empty p orbital adjacent to the aromatic π system; resonance can distribute the charge over the ring. Hyperconjugation can stabilise a tertiary alkyl cation, but it is not the specified aromatic delocalisation.
Why not the others: (A) is ordinary primary alkyl; (B) is tertiary without an adjacent benzene ring; (C) is another primary alkyl cation lacking conjugation.
Key point: Identify the orbital that can overlap with a neighbouring π system.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Equimolar ethanal and propanone compete for a limited amount of NaBH₄ under identical conditions. Early analysis shows faster disappearance of ethanal. Which structural reason best supports this trend?
options: A) The aldehyde carbonyl is less hindered and less alkyl-donated
B) The ketone has no carbonyl carbon
D) Ethanal cannot be reduced at all
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Aldehyde is generally more accessible/electrophilic.
Why: Ethanal has one alkyl substituent and a hydrogen at its carbonyl carbon; propanone has two alkyl groups, increasing steric hindrance and electron donation. Hydride addition can occur to both, but the stated early-rate difference is consistent with a more reactive aldehyde under comparable conditions.
Why not the others: (B) contradicts propanone structure; (C) reverses reducing-agent action; (D) contradicts observed disappearance.
Key point: Compare both steric and electronic effects on carbonyl addition.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: An aryl diazonium chloride is prepared at 0–5 °C. One aliquot couples with alkaline phenol to give an azo dye; a second is warmed with water and releases N₂. Which product is expected from the second aliquot, and why keep the first cold?
options: B) Phenol; cold retains diazonium long enough for coupling
D) Chlorobenzene; cold supplies chloride substitution
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Phenol; cold permits diazonium coupling before hydrolysis.
Why: Diazonium ions are more persistent at low temperature and undergo electrophilic azo coupling with activated phenol. Warming in water promotes replacement of the diazonium group by OH with loss of N₂, furnishing phenol. The two aliquots distinguish competition between coupling and hydrolysis rather than a change of starting aryl skeleton.
Why not the others: (A) predicts reduction absent here; (C) omits hydrolytic OH incorporation; (D) assumes a copper-mediated chloride substitution not supplied.
Key point: Temperature and reagents determine which diazonium pathway dominates.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Complete hydrolysis of a purified tripeptide Gly–Ala–Gly yields which amino-acid counts?
options: D) One of each plus a dipeptide
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Two glycine and one alanine.
Why: Hydrolysis cleaves both peptide bonds but does not change residue identities. The sequence names three residues, with glycine at both ends; complete rather than partial cleavage yields only free amino acids. A residual dipeptide would indicate incomplete reaction.
Why not the others: (A) changes alanine into glycine; (B) reverses multiplicities; (D) retains a bond despite complete hydrolysis.
Key point: Count residues before and after bond cleavage.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A reaction's half-life is 20 min when initial concentration is 0.10 M and remains 20 min when it is 0.20 M. Which order is most consistent under identical conditions?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) First.
Given: Half-life is 20 min at an initial concentration of 0.10 M and also 20 min at 0.20 M.
Formula/Principle: Zero order: \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{[A]_0}{2k}\). First order: \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{\ln2}{k}\). Second order: \(t_{1/2}=\dfrac{1}{k[A]_0}\).
Step 1: Doubling \([A]_0\) leaves the half-life unchanged.
Step 2: Only the first-order expression has no \([A]_0\) in it.
Worked derivation: \[\frac{t_{1/2}(0.20\ \mathrm M)}{t_{1/2}(0.10\ \mathrm M)}=\frac{20}{20}=1=\left(\frac{0.20}{0.10}\right)^{1-n}\Rightarrow n=1\]
Why: In a first-order reaction a constant fraction of the reactant reacts in a given time, so the time to fall to half does not depend on how much is present at the start. This is why radioactive decay has a fixed half-life.
Why not the others: (A) For zero order the half-life would double to 40 min. (B) For second order it would halve to 10 min. (C) For third order it would fall to a quarter, 5 min.
Key point: \(t_{1/2}\propto[A]_0^{\,1-n}\); it is constant only for n = 1.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.sub_topic: Dissolution coupled to supplied complex-formation equilibrium
questions.question: A saturated AgCl solution is in contact with solid AgCl and a reservoir that holds free NH₃ at 1.0 M. Use \(K_{sp}=10^{-10}\) and \([\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}]/([\ce{Ag+}][\ce{NH3}]^2)=10^8\). No chloride is initially added, and free Ag⁺ is negligible compared with its complex. What is the approximate total dissolved silver concentration?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 0.10 M.
Given: \(K_{sp}(\ce{AgCl})=10^{-10}\); \(\dfrac{[\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}]}{[\ce{Ag+}][\ce{NH3}]^2}=10^{8}\); free \([\ce{NH3}]=1.0\ \mathrm M\).
Formula/Principle: Add the two equilibria: \(\ce{AgCl(s) + 2NH3 <=> Ag(NH3)2+ + Cl-}\), with \(K=K_{sp}\times K_f\).
Step 1: \(K=10^{-10}\times10^{8}=10^{-2}\).
Step 2: Let the solubility be s. Then \([\ce{Ag(NH3)2+}]\approx s\) and \([\ce{Cl-}]=s\).
Step 3: \(K=\dfrac{s\times s}{(1.0)^2}=10^{-2}\).
Worked derivation: \[s^2=10^{-2}\Rightarrow s=0.10\ \mathrm M;\qquad[\ce{Ag+}]=\frac{s}{10^{8}(1.0)^2}=10^{-9}\ \mathrm M\ll s\]
Why: Ammonia removes free silver ions by forming the stable complex \(\ce{[Ag(NH3)2]+}\). The dissolving equilibrium of AgCl then shifts forward to replace them, so much more AgCl dissolves than in pure water. Nearly all the dissolved silver is present as the complex, which is why the free silver-ion concentration can be neglected.
Why not the others: (B) \(10^{-5}\ \mathrm M\) is the solubility in pure water, \(\sqrt{K_{sp}}\), with no ammonia. (C) \(10^{-10}\) is the solubility product itself, not a concentration. (D) 1.0 M forgets the square root: \(s^2\), not s, equals \(10^{-2}\).
Key point: For coupled equilibria, multiply the constants and then solve the overall equation.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Acidifying yellow chromate solution gives orange dichromate through \(2CrO₄^{2-}+2H^+\rightleftharpoons Cr₂O₇^{2-}+H₂O\). What happens to chromium oxidation number?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) It remains +6.
Why: In chromate, x+4(−2)=−2 yields x=+6. In dichromate, 2x+7(−2)=−2 yields x=+6 again. The colour shift is an acid-base equilibrium involving oxygen/protons, not an electron-transfer redox event.
Why not the others: (A) invents reduction; (C) invents oxidation; (D) assigns a +3 starting state that chromate does not have.
Key point: Calculate both oxidation states before calling a colour change redox.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: A reaction has ΔH=−40 kJ mol⁻¹ and ΔS=−100 J mol⁻¹ K⁻¹, approximately constant. At what temperatures is it spontaneous at constant pressure?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Only T<400 K.
Given: \(\Delta H=-40\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}}\); \(\Delta S=-100\ \mathrm{J\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}=-0.100\ \mathrm{kJ\,mol^{-1}K^{-1}}\).
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S\); the reaction is spontaneous when \(\Delta G<0\).
Step 1: \(\Delta G=-40-T(-0.100)=-40+0.100T\).
Step 2: \(-40+0.100T<0\).
Worked derivation: \[0.100T<40\Rightarrow T<400\ \mathrm K\]
Why: The reaction gives out heat, which favours it, but it also lowers the entropy, which opposes it. The entropy term is multiplied by temperature, so it matters little at low temperature and takes over at high temperature. Below 400 K the enthalpy term wins; at 400 K the reaction is at equilibrium; above it the reverse reaction is spontaneous.
Why not the others: (A) reverses the inequality. (B) ignores the unfavourable entropy change, which dominates at high temperature. (D) ignores the favourable enthalpy change, which dominates at low temperature.
Key point: ΔH < 0 and ΔS < 0: spontaneous only below T = ΔH/ΔS.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: From the vapour-pressure figure at the marked liquid composition, compare the measured total with the Raoult-law prediction. Which deviation and intermolecular interpretation fit?
options: A) Negative deviation, stronger A–B attraction
B) Ideal behaviour at every composition
C) No conclusion because xB is unknown
D) Positive deviation, weaker A–B attraction
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Positive deviation, weaker A–B attraction.
Given: From the figure: \(x_A=0.25\), so \(x_B=0.75\); \(p_A^\circ=100\ \mathrm{mmHg}\); \(p_B^\circ=60\ \mathrm{mmHg}\); measured total pressure 80 mmHg.
Formula/Principle: Ideal total pressure \(=x_Ap_A^\circ+x_Bp_B^\circ\) (Raoult's law).
Step 1: \(p_{\text{ideal}}=0.25(100)+0.75(60)=25+45=70\ \mathrm{mmHg}\).
Step 2: Measured − ideal \(=80-70=+10\ \mathrm{mmHg}\).
Worked derivation: \[p_{\text{ideal}}=0.25(100)+0.75(60)=70\ \mathrm{mmHg};\qquad80-70=+10\ \mathrm{mmHg}\]
Why: The vapour pressure is higher than Raoult's law predicts, so molecules escape from the mixture more easily than from an ideal one. That happens when the attraction between unlike molecules, A–B, is weaker than the A–A and B–B attractions, as in ethanol with acetone.
Why not the others: (A) A negative deviation would give a pressure below 70 mmHg. (B) Ideal behaviour would give exactly 70 mmHg. (C) \(x_B\) is known, because the two mole fractions add up to 1.
Key point: p(observed) > p(ideal): positive deviation, weaker A–B attractions.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Reductive ozonolysis of a cyclic alkene produces one open-chain molecule with an aldehyde at each end and four methylene groups between them. What starting alkene is consistent?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Cyclohexene.
Why: Cutting the C=C in a six-membered ring opens it into a six-carbon chain with aldehydes at both former alkene carbons: OHC–(CH₂)₄–CHO. A terminal acyclic alkene would produce two separate carbonyl molecules instead of one dialdehyde. The carbon count and single-molecule outcome both matter.
Why not the others: (B) gives separate fragments; (C) yields three intervening methylenes; (D) does not undergo this simple isolated-alkene cleavage.
Key point: Reconnect carbonyl carbons to reconstruct a cleaved ring.

questions.subject: Chemistry
questions.question: Chloroethane is refluxed with sodium iodide in dry acetone. What is the organic product, and what drives the reaction forward?
options: A) Ethene; iodide acts as a strong base
B) Iodoethane; sodium chloride is insoluble in dry acetone and precipitates
C) Ethanol; acetone supplies the –OH group
D) Butane; sodium couples two ethyl groups
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Iodoethane; sodium chloride is insoluble in dry acetone and precipitates.
Why: This is the Finkelstein reaction, a halogen exchange by the SN2 mechanism: \(\ce{CH3CH2Cl + NaI -> CH3CH2I + NaCl}\). Sodium iodide dissolves in dry acetone, but sodium chloride does not. As NaCl forms it precipitates and is removed from the equilibrium, so by Le Chatelier's principle the reaction is pushed forward towards the iodoalkane.
Why not the others: (A) Iodide is a good nucleophile but a very weak base, so it substitutes and does not eliminate HCl to give ethene. (C) Acetone is only the solvent and has no –OH group to give. (D) Coupling of two alkyl groups needs sodium metal (Wurtz reaction), not sodium iodide.
Key point: R–Cl or R–Br + NaI in dry acetone → R–I; the precipitate of NaCl or NaBr drives the reaction.

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The hyperbola x²/9−y²/16=1 has its transverse semiaxis doubled while its conjugate semiaxis stays unchanged. What are the new asymptote slopes?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) ±2/3.
Given: \(\dfrac{x^2}{9}-\dfrac{y^2}{16}=1;\quad a\to2a,\ b\ \text{unchanged}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{asymptotes: }y=\pm\dfrac bax\)
Step 1: \(a=3,\ b=4\)
Step 2: \(a'=2\times3=6,\quad b'=4\)
Worked derivation: \[\text{slopes}=\pm\frac{b'}{a'}=\pm\frac46=\pm\frac23\]
Check: \[\frac{x^2}{36}-\frac{y^2}{16}=0\iff y=\pm\frac46x\]
Why: \(\dfrac{x^2}{a^2}-\dfrac{y^2}{b^2}=0\ \text{gives the asymptotes}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\pm\dfrac43\) (original slopes); (B) \(\pm\dfrac{a'}{b'}=\pm\dfrac32\) (inverted); (D) \(\pm\dfrac ab=\pm\dfrac34\).
Key point: \(\text{slope of asymptote}=\pm\dfrac ba\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Rate of change of a volume
questions.question: The radius of a spherical balloon increases at a steady 0.5 cm s⁻¹. At what rate is its volume increasing at the instant when the radius is 10 cm?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 200π cm³ s⁻¹.
Given: \(\dfrac{dr}{dt}=0.5\ \mathrm{cm\,s^{-1}},\quad r=10\ \mathrm{cm}\)
Formula/Principle: \(V=\dfrac43\pi r^3\Rightarrow\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}\)
Step 1: \(4\pi r^2=4\pi(10)^2=400\pi\ \mathrm{cm^2}\)
Worked derivation: \[\frac{dV}{dt}=400\pi\times0.5=200\pi\ \mathrm{cm^3\,s^{-1}}\]
Check: \[\frac{dV}{dt}=(\text{surface area})\times\frac{dr}{dt}\]
Why: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=\dfrac{dV}{dr}\cdot\dfrac{dr}{dt}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}=50\pi\); (B) \(2\pi r^2\dfrac{dr}{dt}=100\pi\); (C) \(4\pi r^2=400\pi\) (\(\dfrac{dr}{dt}\) omitted).
Key point: \(\dfrac{dV}{dt}=4\pi r^2\,\dfrac{dr}{dt}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Using u=1+x² and transformed integration bounds, what is the exact value of \(\int_0^1 x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) \((2\sqrt2-1)/3\).
Given: \(I=\displaystyle\int_0^1x\sqrt{1+x^2}\,dx\)
Formula/Principle: \(u=1+x^2,\quad du=2x\,dx\)
Step 1: \(x=0\to u=1,\quad x=1\to u=2\)
Step 2: \(I=\dfrac12\displaystyle\int_1^2u^{1/2}\,du=\dfrac12\left[\dfrac23u^{3/2}\right]_1^2\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac13\left(2^{3/2}-1\right)=\frac{2\sqrt2-1}{3}\approx0.609\]
Check: \[\frac{d}{dx}\left[\frac13(1+x^2)^{3/2}\right]=x\sqrt{1+x^2}\]
Why: \(x\,dx=\tfrac12\,du\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\dfrac{2\sqrt2+1}{3}\) (sign at the lower limit); (C) \(2\sqrt2-1\) (factor \(\tfrac13\) omitted); (D) \(\dfrac{\sqrt2-1}{3}\) (\(2^{3/2}\to2^{1/2}\)).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\int f'(x)\,[f(x)]^{n}\,dx=\frac{[f(x)]^{n+1}}{n+1}+C\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.sub_topic: Minimum equivalence completion with a class-count constraint
questions.question: On S={1,2,3,4,5,6}, R contains all diagonal pairs and exactly the additional pairs (1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,5),(5,4). What is the minimum number of ordered pairs that must be added to make R an equivalence relation with exactly two equivalence classes?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Six ordered pairs.
Given: \(S=\{1,\dots,6\};\quad R\supset\text{diagonal}\cup\{(1,2),(2,1),(2,3),(3,2),(4,5),(5,4)\}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{a class of size }s\ \text{needs }s^2\ \text{pairs};\quad\text{merging classes of sizes }a,b\ \text{adds }2ab\ \text{pairs}\)
Step 1: \(\text{transitivity}:\ (1,2),(2,3)\Rightarrow(1,3),(3,1)\ \text{must be added}\Rightarrow2\ \text{pairs}\)
Step 2: \(\text{classes}:\ \{1,2,3\},\ \{4,5\},\ \{6\}\Rightarrow3\ \text{classes}\)
Step 3: \(\text{merge costs}:\ 2(3)(2)=12,\quad2(3)(1)=6,\quad2(2)(1)=4\)
Step 4: \(\text{minimum}:\ \{4,5\}\cup\{6\}\Rightarrow4\ \text{pairs}\)
Worked derivation: \[2+4=6\]
Check: \[\{1,2,3\},\{4,5,6\}:\ 3^2+3^2=18=\underbrace{6+6}_{\text{given}}+6\]
Why: \(\text{existing related elements cannot be separated}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2\) (three classes remain); (C) \(2+6=8\) (merges \(\{1,2,3\}\) with \(\{6\}\)); (D) \(2+12=14\) (merges \(\{1,2,3\}\) with \(\{4,5\}\)).
Key point: \(|R|=\displaystyle\sum s_i^2\)
questions.syllabus_anchor: Relations and functions: equivalence relations; counting

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}\) and let I be the 2×2 identity matrix. For which number k is \(A^2-4A+kI=O\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 3.
Given: \(A=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix},\quad A^2-4A+kI=O\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{compute }A^2\ \text{and compare entries}\)
Step 1: \(A^2=\begin{pmatrix}4+1&2+2\\2+2&1+4\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}5&4\\4&5\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 2: \(4A=\begin{pmatrix}8&4\\4&8\end{pmatrix}\)
Step 3: \(A^2-4A=\begin{pmatrix}-3&0\\0&-3\end{pmatrix}=-3I\)
Worked derivation: \[-3I+kI=O\Rightarrow k=3\]
Check: \[\operatorname{tr}A=4,\ \det A=3:\ A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=O\]
Why: \(\text{a }2\times2\ \text{matrix satisfies }A^2-(\operatorname{tr}A)A+(\det A)I=O\)
Why not the others: (A) \(-3\) (sign: \(A^2-4A=-3I\)); (B) \(4=\operatorname{tr}A\); (D) \(5=(A^2)_{11}\).
Key point: \(k=\det A\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed three independent times. What is the probability of at least one head?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 7/8.
Given: \(3\ \text{independent tosses},\quad P(H)=\tfrac12\)
Formula/Principle: \(P(\ge1H)=1-P(\text{no }H)\)
Step 1: \(P(TTT)=\left(\tfrac12\right)^3=\tfrac18\)
Worked derivation: \[P(\ge1H)=1-\frac18=\frac78\]
Check: \[\frac{\binom31+\binom32+\binom33}{8}=\frac{3+3+1}{8}=\frac78\]
Why: \(\{\ge1H\}=\{TTT\}^c\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\tfrac18=P(TTT)\); (B) \(\tfrac38=P(\text{exactly }1H)\); (C) \(\tfrac34=1-\tfrac14\) (two tosses).
Key point: \(P(\text{at least one})=1-P(\text{none})\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many integers from 1 through 100 are divisible by 2 or 3 but not by 5?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 54.
Given: \(1\le n\le100;\quad(2\mid n\ \text{or}\ 3\mid n)\ \text{and}\ 5\nmid n\)
Formula/Principle: \(|X\cup Y|=|X|+|Y|-|X\cap Y|\)
Step 1: \(2\mid n\ \text{or}\ 3\mid n:\ 50+33-16=67\)
Step 2: \(\text{of these, }5\mid n:\ \left\lfloor\tfrac{100}{10}\right\rfloor+\left\lfloor\tfrac{100}{15}\right\rfloor-\left\lfloor\tfrac{100}{30}\right\rfloor=10+6-3=13\)
Worked derivation: \[67-13=54\]
Check: \[\text{per }30:\ |\{2,3,4,6,8,9,12,14,16,18,21,22,24,26,27,28\}|=16;\ 3\times16=48;\ 91\text{–}100:\ \{92,93,94,96,98,99\}=6;\ 48+6=54\]
Why: \(\text{lcm}(2,5)=10,\ \text{lcm}(3,5)=15,\ \text{lcm}(2,3,5)=30\)
Why not the others: (B) \(67\) (multiples of 5 not removed); (C) \(40\ne54\); (D) \(67-7=60\) (\(13\) miscounted).
Key point: \(|(X\cup Y)\setminus Z|=|X\cup Y|-|(X\cup Y)\cap Z|\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: What is the value of \(\binom{10}{0}+\binom{10}{2}+\binom{10}{4}+\binom{10}{6}+\binom{10}{8}+\binom{10}{10}\)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 512.
Given: \(S=\dbinom{10}{0}+\dbinom{10}{2}+\dots+\dbinom{10}{10}\)
Formula/Principle: \((1+1)^{10}=\displaystyle\sum_{k}\binom{10}{k}=2^{10},\quad(1-1)^{10}=\sum_{k}(-1)^k\binom{10}{k}=0\)
Step 1: \(S_{\text{even}}+S_{\text{odd}}=1024\)
Step 2: \(S_{\text{even}}-S_{\text{odd}}=0\)
Worked derivation: \[S_{\text{even}}=\frac{1024+0}{2}=512\]
Check: \[1+45+210+210+45+1=512\]
Why: \(\text{add the expansions at }x=1\ \text{and}\ x=-1\)
Why not the others: (A) \(2^{10}=1024\) (all coefficients); (C) \(2^{8}=256\); (D) \(2^{10}-1=1023\).
Key point: \(\displaystyle\sum_{k\ \text{even}}\binom nk=2^{n-1}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For which a does the infinite series \(\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(a-1)^n\) converge and have sum 3?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) a=5/3.
Given: \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}(a-1)^n=3\)
Formula/Principle: \(\displaystyle\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}r^n=\frac{1}{1-r},\quad|r|<1\)
Step 1: \(r=a-1\Rightarrow\dfrac{1}{1-(a-1)}=\dfrac{1}{2-a}=3\)
Step 2: \(2-a=\dfrac13\Rightarrow a=\dfrac53\)
Worked derivation: \[r=\frac53-1=\frac23,\quad|r|<1,\quad\frac{1}{1-\frac23}=3\]
Check: \[1+\frac23+\frac49+\dots=3\]
Why: \(|r|<1\ \text{is required for convergence}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=\tfrac13:\ r=-\tfrac23,\ S=\tfrac35\); (B) \(a=\tfrac43:\ r=\tfrac13,\ S=\tfrac32\); (D) \(a=2:\ r=1\ (\text{diverges})\).
Key point: \(S_\infty=\dfrac{1}{1-r}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Define f(x)=(x²−a²)/(x−a) for x≠a and f(a)=b. If f is continuous at a and b=6, find a and the derivative at a.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a=3, f′=1.
Given: \(f(x)=\dfrac{x^2-a^2}{x-a}\ (x\ne a),\quad f(a)=b=6\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{continuity}:\ f(a)=\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)\)
Step 1: \(x\ne a:\ f(x)=\dfrac{(x-a)(x+a)}{x-a}=x+a\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to a}f(x)=2a=6\Rightarrow a=3\)
Step 3: \(f(x)=x+3\ \ \forall x\)
Worked derivation: \[f'(3)=\frac{d}{dx}(x+3)=1\]
Check: \[\frac{f(3+h)-f(3)}{h}=\frac{(6+h)-6}{h}=1\]
Why: \(\text{removable discontinuity filled by }b=2a\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=6:\ 2a=12\ne6\); (B) \(f'=1\ne2\); (C) \(a=6\ \text{and}\ f'=2\ \text{both fail}\).
Key point: \(\dfrac{x^2-a^2}{x-a}=x+a\ \ (x\ne a)\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Let y solve y′+y/x=2x for x>0 with y(1)=1. Find \(\int_1^2 y(x)/x\,dx\).
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 7/6.
Given: \(y'+\dfrac yx=2x,\quad x>0,\quad y(1)=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{I.F.}=e^{\int dx/x}=x\Rightarrow(xy)'=2x^2\)
Step 1: \(xy=\dfrac23x^3+C\)
Step 2: \(y(1)=1:\ 1=\dfrac23+C\Rightarrow C=\dfrac13\)
Step 3: \(\dfrac yx=\dfrac23x+\dfrac{1}{3x^2}\)
Step 4: \(\displaystyle\int_1^2\left(\frac23x+\frac{1}{3x^2}\right)dx=\left[\frac{x^2}{3}-\frac{1}{3x}\right]_1^2\)
Worked derivation: \[\left(\frac43-\frac16\right)-\left(\frac13-\frac13\right)=\frac76\]
Check: \[y=\frac23x^2+\frac{1}{3x}:\ y'+\frac yx=\frac43x-\frac{1}{3x^2}+\frac23x+\frac{1}{3x^2}=2x\]
Why: \(y'+Py=Q\Rightarrow\left(ye^{\int P}\right)'=Qe^{\int P}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac95\ne\tfrac43-\tfrac16\); (C) \(\tfrac{17}{6}\ne\tfrac43-\tfrac16\); (D) \(\tfrac32=\tfrac43+\tfrac16\) (sign of \(\tfrac{1}{3x}\)).
Key point: \(xy=\displaystyle\int2x^2\,dx\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: The planes x+y+z=3 and x−y+z=1 meet along a line. Which parametrisation describes their intersection?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (t,1,2−t).
Given: \(x+y+z=3,\quad x-y+z=1\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{subtract and add the equations}\)
Step 1: \((x+y+z)-(x-y+z)=2\Rightarrow2y=2\Rightarrow y=1\)
Step 2: \(x+z=2\)
Worked derivation: \[x=t\Rightarrow(x,y,z)=(t,\ 1,\ 2-t)\]
Check: \[t+1+2-t=3;\qquad t-1+2-t=1\]
Why: \(\text{direction}=(1,1,1)\times(1,-1,1)=(2,0,-2)\parallel(1,0,-1)\)
Why not the others: (A) \((t,0,3-t):\ x-y+z=3\ne1\); (C) \((t,2,1-t):\ x-y+z=-1\ne1\); (D) \((t,1,3-t):\ x+y+z=4\ne3\).
Key point: \(\text{line of intersection}\parallel\mathbf n_1\times\mathbf n_2\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: For a=(1,0,1) and b=(0,2,0), which unit vector along a×b has positive z component?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (−1/√2,0,1/√2).
Given: \(\mathbf a=(1,0,1),\quad\mathbf b=(0,2,0)\)
Formula/Principle: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=(a_yb_z-a_zb_y,\ a_zb_x-a_xb_z,\ a_xb_y-a_yb_x)\)
Step 1: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b=(0\cdot0-1\cdot2,\ 1\cdot0-1\cdot0,\ 1\cdot2-0\cdot0)=(-2,0,2)\)
Step 2: \(|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|=\sqrt{4+0+4}=2\sqrt2\)
Worked derivation: \[\hat{\mathbf n}=\frac{(-2,0,2)}{2\sqrt2}=\left(-\frac{1}{\sqrt2},\ 0,\ \frac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)\]
Check: \[\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf a=-\frac{1}{\sqrt2}+\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=0;\qquad\hat{\mathbf n}\cdot\mathbf b=0\]
Why: \(\mathbf a\times\mathbf b\perp\mathbf a,\ \mathbf b\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2},0,-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt2}\right)=-\hat{\mathbf n}\) (\(z<0\)); (B) \((1,0,1)=\mathbf a\); (D) \((-1,0,1)\) (\(|\cdot|=\sqrt2\ne1\)).
Key point: \(\hat{\mathbf n}=\dfrac{\mathbf a\times\mathbf b}{|\mathbf a\times\mathbf b|}\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: Random variable X has mean 3 and variance 4. Y=aX+b has mean −1 and variance 36, with a<0. What are a and b?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) a=−3, b=8.
Given: \(E(X)=3,\ \operatorname{Var}(X)=4;\quad Y=aX+b,\ E(Y)=-1,\ \operatorname{Var}(Y)=36,\ a<0\)
Formula/Principle: \(E(aX+b)=aE(X)+b,\quad\operatorname{Var}(aX+b)=a^2\operatorname{Var}(X)\)
Step 1: \(36=4a^2\Rightarrow a=\pm3\Rightarrow a=-3\)
Step 2: \(-1=-3(3)+b\Rightarrow b=8\)
Worked derivation: \[a=-3,\qquad b=8\]
Check: \[E(Y)=-9+8=-1;\qquad\operatorname{Var}(Y)=9\times4=36\]
Why: \(b\ \text{shifts the mean only}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(a=3>0\); (B) \(b=-8:\ E(Y)=-17\); (C) \(a=3>0\).
Key point: \(\sigma_Y=|a|\,\sigma_X\)

questions.subject: Mathematics
questions.question: How many solutions of tan x=sin(2x) are in the closed interval [0,2π]?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 7.
Given: \(\tan x=\sin2x,\quad0\le x\le2\pi\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x}=2\sin x\cos x,\quad\cos x\ne0\)
Step 1: \(\sin x\left(1-2\cos^2x\right)=0\)
Step 2: \(\sin x=0\Rightarrow x=0,\ \pi,\ 2\pi\)
Step 3: \(\cos^2x=\dfrac12\Rightarrow x=\dfrac\pi4,\ \dfrac{3\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{5\pi}{4},\ \dfrac{7\pi}{4}\)
Worked derivation: \[3+4=7\]
Check: \[x=\frac{3\pi}{4}:\ \tan x=-1,\ \sin\frac{3\pi}{2}=-1\]
Why: \(\cos x\ne0\ \text{for all 7 values}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(5\) (end points \(0,\ 2\pi\) omitted); (C) \(3\) (\(\sin x=0\) only); (D) \(6\ne7\).
Key point: \(\text{factorise; do not divide by }\sin x\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Motion in a Straight Line / Motion in a Plane
questions.question: From the same origin at t=0, particle A moves at constant +6 m s⁻¹; particle B starts at rest with constant +2 m s⁻² acceleration. When do they next meet?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 6 s.
Given: \(x_A=6t;\quad x_B=\tfrac12(2)t^2=t^2\ \ (\text{SI})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{meeting}\iff x_A=x_B\)
Step 1: \(6t=t^2\Rightarrow t(t-6)=0\)
Worked derivation: \[t=6\ \mathrm s\ \ (t\ne0)\]
Check: \[x_A=36\ \mathrm m,\quad x_B=36\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(v_B=2t=6\ \text{at }t=3\ \mathrm s:\ \text{maximum separation},\ \text{not meeting}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(3\ \mathrm s\) (\(v_A=v_B\)); (C) \(9\ \mathrm s:\ 54\ne81\); (D) \(12\ \mathrm s:\ 72\ne144\).
Key point: \(\text{equal positions, not equal velocities}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A velocity-time graph rises linearly from 0 to 72 km h⁻¹ in 10 s. What displacement is represented by its triangular area?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 100 m.
Given: \(v:\ 0\to72\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}\ \text{linearly in }10\ \mathrm s\)
Formula/Principle: \(s=\text{area under }v\text{–}t=\tfrac12\,v_{\max}\,t\)
Step 1: \(72\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}=72\times\dfrac{1000}{3600}=20\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)
Worked derivation: \[s=\frac12\times20\times10=100\ \mathrm m\]
Check: \[a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}},\quad s=\tfrac12at^2=\tfrac12(2)(100)=100\ \mathrm m\]
Why: \(\text{units must be consistent before computing the area}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(50\ \mathrm m\); (B) \(72\ \mathrm m\); (D) \(20\times10=200\ \mathrm m\) (\(\tfrac12\) omitted).
Key point: \(1\ \mathrm{km\,h^{-1}}=\dfrac{5}{18}\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A water-filled vessel accelerates upward at 2 m s⁻². What is gauge pressure at depth 0.50 m below its free surface? Use ρ=1000 kg m⁻³, g=10 m s⁻².
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 6000 Pa.
Given: \(a=2\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\ (\text{up}),\quad h=0.50\ \mathrm m,\quad\rho=1000\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}},\quad g=10\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Formula/Principle: \(p=\rho\,(g+a)\,h\)
Step 1: \(g_{\text{eff}}=10+2=12\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}\)
Worked derivation: \[p=1000\times12\times0.50=6000\ \mathrm{Pa}\]
Check: \[\text{column of area }A:\ pA-\rho Ahg=\rho Ah\,a\Rightarrow p=\rho h(g+a)\]
Why: \(\text{the liquid column above the point accelerates upward}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\rho(g-a)h=4000\); (B) \(\rho gh=5000\) (\(a\) ignored); (C) \(5500\).
Key point: \(p=\rho\,(g\pm a)\,h\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: System of Particles and Rotational Motion
questions.question: A uniform disc of original mass M and radius R has a concentric hole of radius R/2 removed. Express remaining body's moment of inertia about the central perpendicular axis in terms of its remaining mass m and R.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (5/8)mR².
Given: \(\text{disc }M,\ R;\quad\text{concentric hole of radius }\dfrac R2;\quad m=\text{remaining mass}\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=I_{\text{disc}}-I_{\text{hole}},\quad I_{\text{disc}}=\tfrac12MR^2\)
Step 1: \(m_{\text{hole}}=\dfrac M4,\quad m=\dfrac{3M}{4}\Rightarrow M=\dfrac{4m}{3}\)
Step 2: \(I_{\text{hole}}=\tfrac12\cdot\dfrac M4\cdot\left(\dfrac R2\right)^2=\dfrac{MR^2}{32}\)
Step 3: \(I=\dfrac{MR^2}{2}-\dfrac{MR^2}{32}=\dfrac{15}{32}MR^2\)
Worked derivation: \[I=\frac{15}{32}\cdot\frac{4m}{3}R^2=\frac58mR^2\]
Check: \[\text{annulus}:\ I=\tfrac12m\left(R^2+\tfrac{R^2}{4}\right)=\tfrac58mR^2\]
Why: \(I\ \text{is additive}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(\tfrac12mR^2\) (solid disc of mass \(m\)); (C) \(\tfrac34mR^2\); (D) \(\tfrac{15}{32}mR^2\) (\(M\) not converted to \(m\)).
Key point: \(I_{\text{annulus}}=\tfrac12m\left(R_1^2+R_2^2\right)\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A heat engine completes a cycle, absorbing 500 J from the hot reservoir and rejecting 300 J to the cold reservoir. Find work per cycle and thermal efficiency.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 200 J, 40%.
Given: \(Q_h=500\ \mathrm J,\quad Q_c=300\ \mathrm J\)
Formula/Principle: \(W=Q_h-Q_c,\quad\eta=\dfrac{W}{Q_h}\)
Step 1: \(W=500-300=200\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\eta=\frac{200}{500}=0.40=40\%\]
Check: \[\eta=1-\frac{Q_c}{Q_h}=1-0.6=0.4\]
Why: \(\Delta U_{\text{cycle}}=0\Rightarrow W=Q_{\text{net}}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(300\ \mathrm J=Q_c,\ \dfrac{Q_c}{Q_h}=60\%\); (C) \(500\ \mathrm J=Q_h\); (D) \(60\%=\dfrac{Q_c}{Q_h}\).
Key point: \(\eta=1-\dfrac{Q_c}{Q_h}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Displacement at which kinetic and potential energies are equal
questions.question: A particle performs simple harmonic motion of amplitude A about x=0. At what distance from the mean position is its kinetic energy equal to its potential energy?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A/√2.
Given: \(\text{SHM, amplitude }A,\quad K=U\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12kx^2,\quad K=\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2),\quad E=\tfrac12kA^2\)
Step 1: \(K=U\Rightarrow\tfrac12k(A^2-x^2)=\tfrac12kx^2\)
Step 2: \(A^2=2x^2\)
Worked derivation: \[x=\frac{A}{\sqrt2}\]
Check: \[U=\tfrac12k\cdot\frac{A^2}{2}=\frac E2,\qquad K=E-U=\frac E2\]
Why: \(K+U=E\ \text{and}\ K=U\Rightarrow U=\dfrac E2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(x=\tfrac A2:\ U=\tfrac E4,\ K=\tfrac{3E}{4}\); (B) \(x=\tfrac A4:\ U=\tfrac{E}{16}\); (D) \(x=\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}A:\ U=\tfrac{3E}{4},\ K=\tfrac E4\).
Key point: \(\dfrac UE=\dfrac{x^2}{A^2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Two coherent waves arrive with geometric path difference λ/2, while source 2 has an initial phase lead of π relative to source 1. What is their interference at that point?
options: A) Complete destructive for equal amplitudes
C) The waves have unequal frequencies
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Constructive for equal amplitudes.
Given: \(\Delta x=\dfrac\lambda2,\quad\phi_0=\pi\ \ (\text{source 2 leads})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\Delta\phi=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\Delta x\pm\phi_0\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}\cdot\dfrac\lambda2=\pi\)
Step 2: \(\Delta\phi=\pi+\pi=2\pi\ \ \text{or}\ \ \pi-\pi=0\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta\phi=0\ (\text{mod }2\pi)\Rightarrow A_{\text{res}}=2A\]
Check: \[I=4I_0\cos^2\frac{\Delta\phi}{2}=4I_0\]
Why: \(\text{both sign choices give a multiple of }2\pi\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\Delta\phi=\pi\ \text{only if }\phi_0=0\); (B) \(\text{coherent}\Rightarrow\text{stable pattern}\); (C) \(\text{coherent}\Rightarrow f_1=f_2\).
Key point: \(\Delta\phi_{\text{total}}=\Delta\phi_{\text{path}}+\Delta\phi_{\text{source}}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.topic: Electric Charges and Fields / Electrostatic Potential
questions.question: From the signed electric-field graph between 0 and 3a, what are V(2a)−V(0) and V(3a)−V(0), respectively?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (−E₀a,0).
Given: \(E_x=+2E_0\ (0<x<a),\quad E_x=-E_0\ (a<x<3a)\)
Formula/Principle: \(V(x)-V(0)=-\displaystyle\int_0^xE_x\,dx'\)
Step 1: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{2a}E_x\,dx=2E_0a-E_0a=E_0a\)
Step 2: \(\displaystyle\int_0^{3a}E_x\,dx=2E_0a-2E_0a=0\)
Worked derivation: \[V(2a)-V(0)=-E_0a,\qquad V(3a)-V(0)=0\]
Check: \[V(a)-V(0)=-2E_0a\ (\text{minimum});\quad V(3a)-V(2a)=+E_0a\]
Why: \(\Delta V=-(\text{signed area under }E_x)\)
Why not the others: (B) \(+E_0a\) (sign of \(\Delta V\)); (C) \((0,-E_0a)\) (order reversed); (D) \(-2E_0a=V(a)-V(0)\).
Key point: \(E_x=-\dfrac{dV}{dx}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Current division in a series–parallel network
questions.question: A 6 Ω resistor and a 3 Ω resistor are connected in parallel, and this combination is in series with a 2 Ω resistor across an ideal 12 V battery. What is the current in the 3 Ω resistor?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2 A.
Given: \(6\ \Omega\parallel3\ \Omega,\ \text{in series with }2\ \Omega;\quad V=12\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(R_p=\dfrac{R_1R_2}{R_1+R_2},\quad I=\dfrac{V}{R_{\text{eq}}},\quad I_{3\Omega}=\dfrac{V_p}{3}\)
Step 1: \(R_p=\dfrac{6\times3}{6+3}=2\ \Omega\)
Step 2: \(R_{\text{eq}}=2+2=4\ \Omega,\quad I=\dfrac{12}{4}=3\ \mathrm A\)
Step 3: \(V_p=IR_p=3\times2=6\ \mathrm V\)
Worked derivation: \[I_{3\Omega}=\frac{6}{3}=2\ \mathrm A\]
Check: \[I_{6\Omega}=\frac66=1\ \mathrm A,\qquad2+1=3\ \mathrm A\]
Why: \(\text{parallel branches share the same voltage}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\ \mathrm A=I_{6\Omega}\); (C) \(3\ \mathrm A=I_{\text{total}}\); (D) \(\dfrac{12}{3}=4\ \mathrm A\) (full 12 V across \(3\ \Omega\)).
Key point: \(I_1=I\,\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: Initially 800 radioactive A nuclei decay to stable B with half-life 2 h. After 4 h all accumulated B is removed; A remains. How many new B nuclei form in the next 2 h?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 100 nuclei.
Given: \(N_A(0)=800,\quad T_{1/2}=2\ \mathrm h;\quad\text{B removed at }t=4\ \mathrm h\)
Formula/Principle: \(N_A(t)=N_A(0)\left(\tfrac12\right)^{t/T_{1/2}};\quad\Delta N_B=-\Delta N_A\)
Step 1: \(N_A(4)=800\times\left(\tfrac12\right)^2=200\)
Step 2: \(N_A(6)=200\times\tfrac12=100\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta N_B=N_A(4)-N_A(6)=200-100=100\]
Check: \[800\to400\to200\to100\]
Why: \(\text{each decay of A gives one B}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(50\); (B) \(200=N_A(4)\); (D) \(400=N_A(2)\).
Key point: \(\text{daughter formed}=\text{parent lost in the interval}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: An ideal inductor L=0.50 H carries 2 A, then its current rises to 4 A. How much extra magnetic energy is stored?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3 J.
Given: \(L=0.50\ \mathrm H,\quad I_i=2\ \mathrm A,\quad I_f=4\ \mathrm A\)
Formula/Principle: \(U=\tfrac12LI^2\)
Step 1: \(U_i=\tfrac12(0.50)(2)^2=1\ \mathrm J\)
Step 2: \(U_f=\tfrac12(0.50)(4)^2=4\ \mathrm J\)
Worked derivation: \[\Delta U=4-1=3\ \mathrm J\]
Check: \[\Delta U=\tfrac12L\left(I_f^2-I_i^2\right)=0.25\times12=3\ \mathrm J\]
Why: \(U\propto I^2\)
Why not the others: (A) \(1\ \mathrm J=U_i\) (or \(\tfrac12L(\Delta I)^2\)); (B) \(2\ \mathrm J\); (C) \(4\ \mathrm J=U_f\).
Key point: \(\Delta U=\tfrac12L\left(I_f^2-I_i^2\right)\ne\tfrac12L(\Delta I)^2\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Image formed by a concave mirror for an object inside the focus
questions.question: An object is placed 10 cm in front of a concave mirror of focal length 15 cm. Where is the image, and what is its nature?
options: A) 30 cm behind the mirror; virtual and magnified
B) 30 cm in front of the mirror; real and magnified
C) 6 cm behind the mirror; virtual and diminished
D) 6 cm in front of the mirror; real and diminished
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 30 cm behind the mirror; virtual and magnified.
Given: \(u=-10\ \mathrm{cm},\quad f=-15\ \mathrm{cm}\ \ (\text{concave})\)
Formula/Principle: \(\dfrac1v+\dfrac1u=\dfrac1f,\quad m=-\dfrac vu\)
Step 1: \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac1f-\dfrac1u=-\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{10}=\dfrac{1}{30}\)
Step 2: \(v=+30\ \mathrm{cm}\ \ (\text{behind the mirror})\)
Worked derivation: \[m=-\frac{30}{-10}=+3\]
Check: \[|u|=10\ \mathrm{cm}<|f|=15\ \mathrm{cm}\Rightarrow\text{virtual, upright, magnified}\]
Why: \(v>0\Rightarrow\text{virtual};\quad m>0\Rightarrow\text{upright};\quad|m|>1\Rightarrow\text{magnified}\)
Why not the others: (B) \(v=+30\ \mathrm{cm}\ne-30\ \mathrm{cm}\); (C) \(\dfrac1v=\dfrac{1}{15}+\dfrac{1}{10}=\dfrac16\) (sign of \(f\)); (D) \(v=-6\ \mathrm{cm}\) (signs of \(f\) and \(u\)).
Key point: \(\text{object inside the focus of a concave mirror}\Rightarrow\text{virtual, magnified image}\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: From the rms phasor diagram for a series circuit, determine the current and whether it leads or lags the supply.
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1 A, lagging.
Given: \(\text{from the phasor diagram}:\ V_R=30\ \mathrm V,\quad R=30\ \Omega,\quad V_L-V_C=+40\ \mathrm V\)
Formula/Principle: \(I=\dfrac{V_R}{R},\quad\tan\phi=\dfrac{V_L-V_C}{V_R}\)
Step 1: \(I=\dfrac{30}{30}=1\ \mathrm A\)
Step 2: \(\tan\phi=\dfrac{40}{30}=\dfrac43>0\Rightarrow\text{voltage leads current}\)
Worked derivation: \[I=1\ \mathrm A,\qquad\phi=\tan^{-1}\frac43\approx53^\circ\ (\text{current lags})\]
Check: \[V=\sqrt{30^2+40^2}=50\ \mathrm V,\quad Z=\frac{50}{1}=50\ \Omega\]
Why: \(V_L>V_C\Rightarrow\text{net inductive}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{50}{30}=\dfrac53\ \mathrm A\) (\(V\) for \(V_R\)), and leading; (C) \(V_L>V_C\Rightarrow\text{lagging}\); (D) \(\dfrac53\ \mathrm A\ne\dfrac{V_R}{R}\).
Key point: \(X_L>X_C:\ I\ \text{lags }V;\quad X_C>X_L:\ I\ \text{leads }V\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.question: A sinusoidal 50 Hz supply feeds ideal half-wave and full-wave rectifiers. What are their output ripple repetition frequencies, half-wave then full-wave?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 50 Hz, 100 Hz.
Given: \(f_{\text{in}}=50\ \mathrm{Hz},\quad T=\dfrac{1}{50}=20\ \mathrm{ms}\)
Formula/Principle: \(\text{half-wave: one pulse per cycle};\quad\text{full-wave: two pulses per cycle}\)
Step 1: \(\text{half-wave}:\ T_{\text{out}}=T=20\ \mathrm{ms}\)
Step 2: \(\text{full-wave}:\ T_{\text{out}}=\dfrac T2=10\ \mathrm{ms}\)
Worked derivation: \[f_{\text{half}}=\frac{1}{20\ \mathrm{ms}}=50\ \mathrm{Hz},\qquad f_{\text{full}}=\frac{1}{10\ \mathrm{ms}}=100\ \mathrm{Hz}\]
Check: \[|\sin\omega t|\ \text{has period}\ \frac{\pi}{\omega}=\frac T2\]
Why: \(\text{full-wave output}\propto|\sin\omega t|\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\text{order reversed}\); (B) \(f_{\text{full}}=2f_{\text{in}}\ne50\ \mathrm{Hz}\); (D) \(f_{\text{half}}=f_{\text{in}}\ne100\ \mathrm{Hz}\).
Key point: \(f_{\text{ripple}}=f\ (\text{half-wave}),\ 2f\ (\text{full-wave})\)

questions.subject: Physics
questions.sub_topic: Malus's law with unpolarised incident light
questions.question: Unpolarised light of intensity I₀ passes through a polariser and then through an analyser whose axis makes 60° with that of the polariser. Both are ideal. What is the intensity of the light that emerges?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) I₀/8.
Given: \(\text{unpolarised }I_0;\quad\theta=60^\circ\)
Formula/Principle: \(I_1=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\ (\text{polariser}),\quad I_2=I_1\cos^2\theta\ (\text{Malus})\)
Step 1: \(I_1=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\)
Step 2: \(\cos^260^\circ=\dfrac14\)
Worked derivation: \[I_2=\frac{I_0}{2}\times\frac14=\frac{I_0}{8}\]
Check: \[\theta=0:\ I_2=\frac{I_0}{2};\qquad\theta=90^\circ:\ I_2=0\]
Why: \(\langle\cos^2\theta\rangle=\tfrac12\ \text{for unpolarised light}\)
Why not the others: (A) \(\dfrac{I_0}{2}=I_1\) (analyser ignored); (B) \(I_0\cos^260^\circ=\dfrac{I_0}{4}\) (first \(\tfrac12\) omitted); (C) \(\dfrac{I_0}{2}\sin^260^\circ=\dfrac{3I_0}{8}\).
Key point: \(I=\dfrac{I_0}{2}\cos^2\theta\)
